newsitem.title: INDIA: India urged to hasten oil sector reforms.
newsitem.headline: India urged to hasten oil sector reforms.

text.p: India must speed up oil industry reforms and set up a vigorous regulatory mechanism to attract private investors into the sector, experts said on Thursday.

"India must dismantle the administered price mechanism (APM) at a much faster pace than the currently envisaged targets," Rajendra Pachouri, head of the independent Tata Energy Research Institute (TERI), told Reuters.
India, which launched a wide-ranging programme of economic reforms in 1991, set up an official panel which recommended the phased reform of the oil sector over a six-year period.
Analysts have criticised the state-administered oil price mechanism, saying it causes distortions in consumer prices, large subsidies on key products and a lack of competition.

The country's demand for petroleum products is expected to rise to 150 million tonnes by the turn of the century and to 190 million tonnes by 2010. More than half of India's current annual demand of about 70 million tonnes is met by imports.
"I would say we should go the whole hog in the next two or three years," said Pachouri. "Six years is too long. The world is not going to wait that long."
Increasing the pace of reform would send important signals to foreign investors and bring larger investments into the downstream sector, he said.

Experts at an oil conference that ended here on Wednesday said India needed a comprehensive energy policy to exploit domestic resources and must speed up deregulation and market reforms to become globally competitive.
The conference, organised by TERI, recommended that India intensify its exploration and production efforts and that the international community be told of the opportunities in India.

"India and Pakistan are markets that are left behind in the region," said Fereidun Fesharaki, director of the programme on resources at the East-West Center in Hawaii. "India is four or five years behind and has to catch up."

Conference delegates said India must create a regulatory mechanism to ensure the equitable and efficient flow of capital to the hydrocarbon sector and give the regulatory body powers to make decisions quickly and transparently.
"The government must set up a regulatory mechanism quickly for the downstream and upstream sectors," Pachouri said.
Asia was a growth market for investors as demand for energy in industrialised countries was rising slowly, Pachouri said.

Investors were disillusioned with China and focusing more on Indonesia. Bangladesh, with its abundant gas reserves, would be fairly attractive for oil companies. Delegates said India must move quickly on its liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects and iron out problems with its neighbours to ease pipeline transportation of imported gas.
They urged India and rival Pakistan to establish gas pipeline links with the gas-rich countries of the Middle East to boost the subcontinent's economic growth.
Since 1994 India has sought pipelines to import gas from the Middle East, especially Oman and Iran. But technical and political problems have stalled their progress.

Delegates said Pakistan's reluctance to permit an offshore route survey had frustrated work on the feasibility of the project, because the planned pipeline would have to pass through Pakistani territorial waters.
"We have to maintain our diplomatic initiatives to see that pumping of natural gas from neighbouring countries becomes a reality," Pachouri said.
